events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. Black Birth Joy Thursday, October 1, 2026 – Friday, January 15, 2027 Lane Hall Exhibit Space, 204 S State St., Ann Arbor, MI Open M–F, 9AM–5PM

They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

events.title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
events.summary: Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering. As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting? On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.
events.imageAlt: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: Relaxed Open Rehearsal: Sheléa Sings Aretha Franklin
events.summary: Hands-on activities are available from 12:30–1:30 PM. This free, relaxed open rehearsal gives you a behind-the-scenes look at the DSO as the musicians prepare for the weekend's concerts. Join GRAMMY®-nominated vocal powerhouse Sheléa in an evening celebrating the music of Aretha Franklin. Featuring classic hits including “Chain of Fools,” “Say A Little Prayer,” “Respect,” and “Natural Woman,” Sheléa brings the music of Aretha Franklin to life with her one-of-a-kind voice and masterful piano skills. "Relaxed" events are designed for individuals on the autism spectrum and with other sensory sensitivities. Our culture can be unforgiving if you're unable to conform to the standard concert etiquette of quietly sitting still for extended periods. This excludes individuals who are unable to sit still or who may express emotions such as joy or excitement through vocalization. This relaxed open rehearsal aims to remove barriers, allowing everyone to be themselves and enjoy a musical experience in a safe and judgement-free environment. Your experience includes: • Exclusive access to a DSO rehearsal; • Limited audience size for reduced crowds; • A sensory toolkit with noise-cancelling headphones and fidgets for use during the rehearsal (limited number available); • Quiet Space to take a break; • Pre-rehearsal activities; • Complimentary parking; • Trained DSO staff members—the Mid-Michigan Autism Association has provided training to our staff to help them better understand the characteristics of autism and how to better communicate with someone with autism; • Resources to help you prepare for the event, including an information guide, social story, and Spotify playlist. American Sign Language interpretation is offered at this event. Questions? Reach out to Kiersten Alcorn, Manager of Engagement & Accessibility, at accessibility@dso.org.

events.title: Comics Beyond Sight
events.summary: This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening. View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: LRCCS Noon Lecture Series | China’s Economic Slowdown: A Firm-Level Perspective
events.summary: Please note: This lecture will be held in person and virtually on Zoom. If you would like to attend via Zoom, registration is required. Once you've registered, joining information will be sent to your email. Register for the Zoom webinar at: https://myumi.ch/DW8j6 This talk develops a new representative firm-level dataset for Chinese manufacturing from 1998 to 2019 by combining tax, registry, and inspection records and correcting for sampling biases in existing administrative data. Using a CES production framework with firm-specific distortions, the talk introduces a novel decomposition of aggregate TFP growth into efficient growth and changes in misallocation. The analysis documents a sharp slowdown in Chinese manufacturing productivity growth after 2010, driven both by weaker incumbent-firm productivity growth and by a diminished contribution from firm turnover and reallocation. Loren Brandt is a professor of economics at the University of Toronto specializing in the Chinese economy. He has published widely on the Chinese economy in leading economic journals including the *American Economic Review*, *the Quarterly Journal of Economics*, *Review of Economic Studies*, *Econometrica and the Journal of Political Economy*, and been involved in extensive household and enterprise survey work in both China and Vietnam. With Thomas Rawski, he completed *Policy, Regulation, and Innovation in China’s Electricity and Telecom Industries* (Cambridge University Press, 2019), an interdisciplinary effort analyzing the effect of government policy on the power and telecom sectors in China. He was also co-editor and major contributor to *China’s Great Economic Transformation* (Cambridge University Press, 2008), which provides an integrated analysis of China’s unexpected economic boom of the past three decades. His current research focuses on issues of entrepreneurship and firm dynamics, industrial policy and innovation, and economic growth and structural change.

events.title: DCMB Tools and Technology Seminar by Akhil Kondepudi (Computational Medicine & Bioinformatics)
events.summary: Join us for the DCMB Tools & Technology Seminar Series featuring a presentation by Akhil Kondepudi from the Department of Computational Medicine & Bioinformatics. Enjoy a complimentary pizza lunch while learning about innovative research and cutting-edge tools. Associated Article: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04497-1 Abstract Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models have advanced rapidly through training on internet-scale public data, yet such systems lack access to private clinical data. Neuroimaging is underrepresented in the public domain due to identifiable facial features within magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) scans, restricting model performance in clinical medicine. Here we show that frontier models underperform on neuroimaging tasks and that learning directly from uncurated data generated during routine clinical care at health systems, a paradigm we call ‘health system learning’, yields high-performance, generalist neuroimaging models. We introduce NeuroVFM, a visual foundation model trained on 5.24 million clinical MRI and CT volumes using a scalable volumetric predictive architecture. NeuroVFM learns comprehensive representations of brain anatomy and pathology, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple clinical tasks, including radiologic diagnosis and report generation. The model embeds MRI and CT scans into a shared neuroanatomic latent space and grounds diagnostic findings. When paired with open-source language models, NeuroVFM generates radiology reports that surpass frontier models in accuracy, clinical triage and expert preference. NeuroVFM reduces hallucinated findings and critical errors, offering safer clinical decision support. These results establish health system learning as a paradigm for building generalist medical AI and provide a scalable framework for clinical foundation models.

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: Piano Master Class with Ran Dank & Soyeon Kate Lee
events.summary: The Department of Piano hosts a piano master class featuring guest artists Ran Dank (Eastman) and Soyeon Kate Lee (Juilliard). Free and open to the public. ABOUT THE GUEST ARTISTS RAN DANK *Technically dazzling and intellectually probing artistry exemplify Ran Dank‘s pianism and musicality – captivating audiences and critics alike.* Recent season has included performances with the Pasadena Symphony and Keitaro Harada, Monterey Symphony, and Westchester Philharmonic with Jayce Ogren. Ran’s past performances have included recitals at the San Francisco Performances Series, Gilmore, Ravinia, Carnegie Hall’s Zankel and Weill Halls, Steinway Hall, Gardner Museum, Kennedy Center, Town Hall, Yale School of Music, Philips Collection, Morgan Library, Pro Musica in San Miguel de Allende, Mexico, Portland Ovations, and have garnered critical acclaim from the New York Times and The Washington Post. Mr. Dank has performed as a soloist with the orchestras of Cleveland, Sydney, St. Luke’s, Portland, Eugene, Toledo, Hawaii, Kansas City, Vermont, Charleston, Jerusalem, Valencia, Phoenix, Hilton Head, among others, working under the batons such as Michael Stern, Jahja Ling, Michael Christie, Kirill Karabits, Jun Märkl, Pinchas Zukerman, Jorge Mester, Jaime Laredo, and Ken-David Masur. Mr. Dank’s recent performance of the monumental set of variations *The People United Will Never Be Defeated!* at the University of Chicago has been selected as one of the top ten performances of 2017 by the *Chicago Classical Review*. Mr. Dank is an ardent advocate for contemporary music, and has performed in recent seasons Kevin Puts’ piano concerto *Night*, the Tobias Picker concerto, *Keys to the City*, Frederic Rzewski’s *The People United Will Never Be Defeated*, William Bolcom’s Pulitzer winning set of *Twelve New Etudes*, and has given, alongside pianist and wife, Soyeon Kate Lee, the world premieres of Frederic Rzewski’s *Four Hands*, and Alexander Goehr’s *Seven Impromptus*. Mr. Dank and Soyeon Kate lee have also featured the world premiere of multiple grammy-nominated pianist and composer’s Marc-André Hamelin’s "Tango” for piano four-hands. The recipient of numerous honors, Ran Dank won a coveted place on the Young Concert Artists roster in 2009 and subsequently made his New York recital debut. He was a laureate of the Cleveland International Competition, the Naumburg Piano Competition, the Sydney International Piano Competition, and the Hilton Head International Piano Competition. Mr. Dank serves as an Associate Professor of Piano at the Eastman School of Music. His mentors and teachers include Emanuel Ax, Richard Goode, Joseph Kalichstein, Julian Martin, Robert McDonald, and Ursula Oppens. SOYEON KATE LEE First prize winner of the Naumburg International Piano Competition and the Concert Artist Guild International Competition, Korean-American pianist Soyeon Kate Lee has been lauded by *The New York Times* as a pianist with “a huge, richly varied sound, a lively imagination and a firm sense of style,” and by the *Washington Post* for her “stunning command of the keyboard.” Highlights of recent seasons include appearances at the National Gallery, Library of Congress, Gina Bachauer Concerts, Purdue Convocations, Music@Menlo, Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center on tour, San Francisco Performances, Camerata Pacifica tour, Chamber Music Chicago, and the Cleveland Art Museum. She was a member of Lincoln Center Chamber Music Society’s Bowers program, and is a regular participant in numerous chamber music festivals including the Great Lakes, Santa Fe and Music Mountain Chamber Music Festivals. Ms. Lee has collaborated with conductors Carlos Miguel Prieto, Rafael Frühbeck de Burgos, Jahja Ling, and Jorge Mester with the London, San Diego, Hawaii, Louisiana, Naples symphony orchestras among others. She has commissioned works by prominent composers and has given world premieres of works written by Frederic Rzewski, Paola Prestini, Marc-André Hamelin, Alexander Goehr, Gabriela Lena Frank, Texu Kim, and Huang Ruo. As a Naxos recording artist, her discography spans a wide range of repertoire from two volumes of Scarlatti Sonatas, Liszt Opera Transcriptions, two volumes of Scriabin, and Clementi Sonatas. Ms. Lee’s recording of *Re!nvented* under the E1/Entertainment One (formerly Koch Classics) label garnered her a feature review in the *Gramophone* Magazine and the Classical Recording Foundation’s Young Artist of the Year Award. A second prize and Mozart Prize winner of the 2003 Cleveland International Piano Competition and a laureate of the Santander International Piano Competition in Spain, she is a graduate of the Juilliard School where she was awarded the William Petschek Piano Debut Award at Lincoln Center and the Arthur Rubinstein Award upon graduation, and received her Doctor of Musical Arts from The Graduate Center, City University of New York. Her major mentors and teachers have been Richard Goode, Julian Martin, Robert McDonald, Jerome Lowenthal, and Ursula Oppens. In 2022, Soyeon Kate Lee joined the piano faculty at the Juilliard School, and serves on the piano faculty at the Bowdoin International Music Festival during the summers. She resides in New York with her husband, pianist Ran Dank, and their two children, Noah and Ella.

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: Nothing Without Us: A Messy Path to Youth-Governed Programmable Media
events.summary: This is a hybrid in-person/remote event. Zoom link for remote attendance: https://umich.zoom.us/j/98784211378?pwd=wsTRehTTNgggSbXgfYPyjEnAhfEbvI.1 For in-person attendees, a reception with refreshments will follow the lecture at 4:30 on the third floor of the Beyster Building. ABSTRACT: For most of the history of computing, computer scientists and software engineers have been in charge of what computing the world uses. Even human-computer interaction, a field that starts from the premise that technologists often do not know what people want or need, has positioned designers as the deciders, on behalf of the world. And yet, for decades, scholars, activists, and democracies have shown that the only way to build futures that work for everyone is to involve everyone. What happens when we try to transfer power away from computer scientists to stakeholders, especially when the ability to create software appears to be rapidly democratizing? I report on five years of trying (and often failing) to share power in the specific domain of educational programming language design with middle schoolers and their teachers. Across interactions with hundreds of youth and young adults, spanning a wide range of abilities, natural language fluencies, races, ethnicities, cultures, genders, and human values, I share the joint design decisions we have made, the surprising innovations and discoveries that emerged from them, and the many open questions we’ve found on how to jointly shape the future of computing. I also reflect on the challenges of creating models for youth governance that balance computer science expertise with the unrestrained creativity of youth and declining public support for such research. BIO: Amy J. Ko is a Professor at the University of Washington Information School with courtesy appointments in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science and Engineering and the College of Education (courtesy). She co-directs the UW Center for Learning, Computing, and Imagination, where she studies computing education, human-computer interaction, software engineering, and humanity's individual and collective struggle to equitably use or resist computing for equity, justice, and liberation. With her collaborators, she's invented programming languages and tools to support debugging, program understanding, reuse, and learning; founded and sold a venture-backed startup focused on software troubleshooting; developed numerous ways to weave equity and justice into computing education pedagogy, culture, and technology; and impacted local, state, and federal K-12 CS education policy through community organizing and advocacy. Her work spans more than 160 peer-reviewed publications, with 24 receiving distinguished paper awards and 6 receiving most influential paper awards. She is an ACM Distinguished Member and a member of the SIGCHI Academy for her substantial contributions to the field of human-computer interaction, computing education, and software engineering. She received her Ph.D. at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University in 2008, and degrees in Computer Science and Psychology with Honors from Oregon State University in 2002.

events.title: Mustard's Retreat w/sg Jonas Berzanskis
events.summary: CD release show! May 1975. It seemed inevitable. Libby Glover, Michael Hough and David Tamulevich had been informally jamming with each other for 3 months in the Rathskellar of the Old Heidelberg Restaurant in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The room had grown consistently packed with enthusiastic fans every weekend. They all agreed it was time the trio made it official and chose the name Mustard’s Retreat, which was a tune David had written. Mustard’s Retreat has always sung the songs they enjoyed and cared about, regardless of the trends of the music industry and pop culture. They are committed to simply being themselves, not chasing fame or brass rings, while delighting in and connecting with their audiences as if they were family. The honesty of what they present onstage and the extensive body of outstanding original songs and recordings all contribute to a fiercely loyal audience that continues to grow. “Music to cure what ails you” was how one reviewer in the 1970s described them, and that is as true now as it was then. They’ve traveled more than a million miles and performed more than 6,000 shows, from pig roasts and pool parties to Lincoln Center Out of Doors, The Barns at Wolftrap and the Kennedy’s Center’s Millennium Stage. Tonight the trio reunites to celebrate the release of their new CD, Between Black & White Clouds. Please note this is an afternoon performance with a start time of 3pm!

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.summary: Seminar Summary - Habitat in the landscape plays a key role for conservation and insect-mediated ecosystem services. events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

Enjoy no cover , our full dinner menu, wine specials, plus a special $95 Dinner for Two with your choice of 1 appetizer, 2 entrees, and 1 dessert to share. Noah Hogan is a guitarist and composer based in New York City, whose music draws from the worlds of jazz and Brazilian music. Raised in Ann Arbor, Michigan, Noah was immersed in music from a young age, and began performing at venues across Michigan at age nine. He has since made a name for himself as both a bandleader and sideman on stages across the US and abroad, including Le Duc Des Lombards in Paris, Beco das Garrafas in Rio De Janeiro, DROM in NYC, Cliff Bell’s in Detroit, and the Blue LLama Jazz Club in Ann Arbor. A versatile guitarist, he has also provided guitar for off-Broadway productions, and his playing can be heard on several recorded projects of various styles. A recipient of a Fulbright Award in 2025, Noah spent nine months living in Rio de Janeiro, exploring the traditional music styles of Brazil, from samba and choro, to forró and maracatú. He returns with an evolved musical and compositional voice, drawing from the rich rhythms, harmonies, and melodies he encountered there. Inspired by the likes of Milton Nascimento, Toninho Horta, Esperanza Spalding, and Pat Metheny, Noah aims to create a unique sound that is distinctly his own, while honoring the traditions that shaped it. events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: From Code to Composition: Personalized Recommendations and Product Innovation (joint with Maria Trejos, Diana Van Patten, and Kai Hao)
events.summary: This paper studies how personalized recommendation algorithms (PRAs), a central application of artificial intelligence, shape product innovation. We develop an equilibrium model in which consumers have heterogeneous tastes, producers choose product characteristics subject to costs, and a platform recommends products while learning preferences from noisy signals. Personalization changes producers' incentives by allowing them to target different consumer segments. This response can increase market-wide differentiation and make new products more distinct from the existing stock, even when personalization narrows individual exposure. We examine these implications in the music industry, where PRAs have been widely adopted since the mid-2010s. Using tools from music information retrieval applied to raw audio files, we find that songs have become more original, both within a given year and relative to past releases, following the widespread adoption of PRAs. We extend the model to CES preferences and combine our originality estimates with listening-time shares to quantify the welfare implications. The implied consumer-surplus gains associated with additional originality range from 2.2% to 2.4% in 2023 relative to a counterfactual with originality fixed at its 2013 level.

events.title: Comics Beyond Sight
events.summary: This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening. events.title: CM-AMO Seminar | Magnetism and Superconductivity in the Bilayer Nickelates
events.summary: The bilayer nickelate La3Ni2O7 was recently discovered to superconduct at temperatures above 80 K, when placed under large hydrostatic pressures. While these newly-discovered nickelates share some common features to the copper oxide superconductors, they also have some important differences as well, making them a natural test for ideas surrounding high-temperature superconductivity. In this talk, I will introduce this new class of superconductors, and how we are able to stabilize superconductivity in this material at ambient pressure using molecular beam epitaxy and compressive strain in epitaxial thin films to mimic the effects of pressure. I will then address a key question about the origin of superconductivity in these materials, namely the relationship between magnetic order and superconductivity, which plays a critical role in other families of high-temperature superconductors such as the cuprates and Fe-based superconductors.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

events.title: Aviram Reichert Piano Master Class
events.summary: Guest pianist Aviram Reichert (Seoul National University) will present a master class for talented students from the SMTD piano performance programs. ABOUT THE GUEST ARTIST Acclaimed for his deeply intelligent interpretations, phenomenal technique and ravishing tone – AVIRAM REICHERT won the Bronze Medal at the 10th Van Cliburn International Piano Competition in 1997, after winning several major competitions in Japan, Korea, France, and Germany. His accomplishments brought him numerous concert engagements in the Asia, the United States, South Africa, Europe and Israel where he has been earning immense applause for 30 years. Following a performance of Brahms’s first piano concerto and Manuel de Falla’s evocative *Nights in the Gardens of Spain* with the Grand Rapids Symphony under the baton of David Lockington, Reichert was described as “a big player with all the tension of a coiled spring suddenly unsprung….He has heft and he has poetry.” With over 30 concerti in his repertoire Reichert performs frequently with leading orchestras in the USA, Israel, Japan, Korea and South Africa. He has been regularly featured artist at Durango’s Music in the Mountains festival, performing concerti and chamber music for over 25 years. Reichert has performed throughout the United States, Israel, South Africa, Asia, and in Europe, where an appearance at the Herkules-Saal in Munich elicited an enthusiastic “ovation” and high critical praise. Festival performances include the Ruhr and Epinal Music Festivals, Tokyo Summer Festival, Seoul Spring Festival, Bear Valley CA, Durango and Steamboat Springs CO, Ravinia Festival, the Fontana and the Gilmore Keyboard Festivals. A fine chamber musician, he has collaborated with artists such as Anne Akiko Meyers, Maya Beiser, Guy Braunstein, Yuri Gandelsman, Vadim Gluzman, Dylana Jenson, Bill Purcell and Philippe Quint. Reichert can be heard on a Harmonia Mundi CD featuring highlights of his prize-winning solo performances at the Van Cliburn Competition, a Jerusalem Music Center label (JMC) featuring Schubert sonatas, a Mozart concerti CD with the Music in the Mountains Festival Orchestra, conducted and performed from the keyboard. He has also recorded Gershwin’s *Rhapsody in Blue* with the Spectrum Brass, Brahms cello sonatas with Young Hoon Song and Brahms clarinet sonatas and songs with Ron Selka. In addition to his busy concert career, Reichert is a sought-after teacher, who is frequently invited to conduct masterclasses in Japan, China, Korea, South Africa, France, Israel and the United States. He is Artistic Director at the prestigious Tel Hai International Piano Masterclasses in Israel and a Professor of Piano at Seoul National University, College of Music, where his students won numerous local and international awards. A Steinway artist, he studied the Rubin Academy of Music, Tel Aviv with Professor Arie Vardi.

She has performed internationally, including at all the major Canadian festivals, Tucson Jazz Festival, Tokyo’s famed Cotton Club, Live From Emmett’s Place , and featured with Orchestre national de jazz de Montréal and UMO Helsinki Jazz Orchestra in Finland. Gyorgy is currently signed to Brooklyn label La Reserve Records and has released five albums of original and standard music, including her three JUNO award-winning albums Now Pronouncing , Featuring, Hello! How Are You? , and her 2024 JUNO-nominated album with pianist Mark Limacher You’re Alike, You Two . As a collaborator, she has recorded and performed with musicians including Christine Jensen, Laila Biali, Jocelyn Gould, Ira Coleman, Bryn Roberts and Pat LaBarbera. In addition to being a performer, Gyorgy is an avid writer and composes songs in the style of the Great American Songbook. Her compositions have been sung by other vocalists around the world, and have won multiple awards including the Grand Prize in the jazz category of the 2021 John Lennon Songwriting Contest. Gyorgy is also a sought after clinician and is currently on faculty as a vocal jazz instructor at the Yukon Summer Music Camp in Whitehorse, Yukon and the Interprovincial Music Camp in McKellar, Ontario. Her strong social media presence also sees her utilising platforms like Instagram (83k followers) and TikTok (122k followers) to engage with the next generation of jazz students, encouraging them to scat with her or join her, virtually, in the recording studio. Her album “Hello! How Are You?” features Gyorgy accompanied by her regular piano trio and was released in August, 2024. It was the 2025 JUNO Award-winner for “Best Jazz Album of the Year”. Her upcoming album “Asking For Trouble” is out 11 April 2025 on La Reserve Records and features pianist Mark Limacher. The duo celebrates the music of the incomparable composer and lyricist Frank Loesser. Check out her interview with WEMU. RESERVE TABLE

events.title: The Borderland Ensemble
events.summary: Sat | Jan 30 Sets 7pm & 9pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE About the Artist The Borderland Ensemble is a cross-border jazz collective based in the Windsor-Detroit region, led by trumpeter and composer Austin Di Pietro. For the 2026 Detroit Jazz Festival, the ensemble features Alex Colista on alto saxophone, Tom Bartelmay on guitar, Aya Sekine on piano, Trevor Lamb on bass, and Zachary McKinney on drums. The group draws on its unique geography – two cities, two countries, sharing one river – as both subject matter and creative fuel. The ensemble plays original music rooted in the jazz tradition and shaped by the sounds of this particular corner of the world: hard bop and post-bop at the foundation, with more contemporary influences woven throughout. The music explores what it means to make art across a border at a moment when that border feels more fraught than ever – treating division not as an obstacle, but as a source of creative possibility. The group’s Detroit Jazz Festival debut arrives in support of its first album, Live at Mackenzie Hall Jazz, which was released July 3, 2026. Performing at the world-renowned jazz festival – situated just steps from the Detroit River and international boundary – is a natural extension of the cross-border conversation the ensemble was built around. RESERVE TABLE

events.title: Charlene Kaye in Diversity Shredder
events.summary: Welcome to the unhinged, razor-sharp, fluorescent universe of Charlene Kaye : guitar god, internet legend and “breakout comedy star” according to Rolling Stone. Known for her countless viral videos such as “Every Taylor Swift Song” (100M views and counting), she brings us a brand new show: Diversity Shredder! Kaye has been touring her critically acclaimed debut show "Tiger Daughter: Or, How I Brought My Immigrant Mother Ultimate Shame," presented by comedy icon Margaret Cho. That show played to sold-out runs at Edinburgh Fringe 2024 and Melbourne International Comedy Festival 2025, and it will soon be filmed as her first comedy special. While Tiger Daughter was a hilarious and heartfelt hour about her mother, Diversity Shredder is a madcap musical about being a menace to society as an Asian woman guitar shredder. From starting out as a folk singer-songwriter, to shredding in wizard rock band Team StarKid, to starting endless gender-flipped cover bands like Guns N’ Hoses and Labiahead, it’s an unhinged tour of her musical universe. You’ll be rolling in your seats, you’ll learn a lot about how music works, and you might even confuse her for Bobby Lee. Anything is possible!

events.title: CMENAS 2026 Fall Colloquium Series | The Israeli Elections of 10/27/2026: Outcomes and Implications
events.summary: Professor Yael Aronoff will discuss key issues surrounding the Israeli elections that took place on October 27th, 2026. Her analysis will include looking back on the array of opposition parties to the Benjamin Netanyahu’s government over the past four years, and the constellation of old and new political parties competing in the elections; she will also examine the results of the election, the potential government coalitions or actual coalitions formed, and consider the implications for a variety of Israeli domestic policies, including the possibilities of democratic backsliding or strengthening, the impact on relations with Palestinians, prospects for a two-state solution, and the implications for Israel’s relations with its neighbors and with the United States. Yael Aronoff [Ph.D. PLS, Columbia U.] is the Director of the Michael and Elaine Serling Institute for Jewish Studies and Modern Israel (since 2014), is the Michael and Elaine Serling and Friends Chair of Israel Studies (since 2006) and is Professor of Political Science/International Relations in James Madison College at MSU. Dr. Aronoff was President of the Association of Israel Studies (2019-2021), a recipient of the MSU 2011 Teacher-Scholar Award, and the recipient of the 2015 MSU John K. Hudzik Emerging Leader in Advancing International Studies and Programs Award. Dr. Aronoff’s published books are The Political Psychology of Israeli Prime Ministers: When Hard-Liners Opt for Peace, Cambridge University Press (2014) and Continuity and Change in Political Culture: Israel and Beyond, co-edited with Ilan Peleg and Saliba Sarsar, Lexington Books (2021). Her recent publications include chapters in edited books about the Israeli opposition parties and analyses of Netanyahu, including “The Impact of October 7th and its Aftermath on Israel’s Zionist Opposition Parties,” in The Impact of the Israel-Hamas War on Israeli Domestic Politics, Security Policy and Foreign Policy, Ed. Robert O. Freedman,” forthcoming, DeGruyter-Brill, spring 2027. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. Black Birth Joy Thursday, October 1, 2026 – Friday, January 15, 2027 Lane Hall Exhibit Space, 204 S State St., Ann Arbor, MI Open M–F, 9AM–5PM

Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. events.title: Linguistics MLK Colloquium
events.summary: The 2027 Linguistics MLK Colloquium will occur on Friday, January 22, 2027, with J. Michael Terry as the speaker. J. Michael Terry is an Associate Professor in the Department of Linguistics, and adjunct in the Department of African, African American, and African Diaspora Studies at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. His work focuses on dialects of American English, especially African American English (AAE). Although he works primarily in tense and aspect semantics, his research employs a mix of methods that includes statistical analysis, formal modeling and EEG (brainwave) measurement techniques. He has written on the topics such as the semantics of AAE tense/aspect markers, single-speaker level language variation, quantifying the use of style-shift in African American adolescents, and, most recently, how dialectal differences can affect non-Mainstream English speaking 2nd graders’ performance on tests of mathematical reasoning. Colloquium Title: What Speakers Do with Done: Pragmatics, Persistence, and Speaker Agency in African American English Abstract: The social and grammatical structures that speakers inherit from their surroundings constrain how they express themselves. Neither, however, fully determines that expression, as neither social conditions nor grammar uses language. Speakers do. In making linguistic choices about what to say, when, and how, speakers simultaneously navigate the constraints these structures pose and draw on the resources they provide to make meaning. Because linguists are typically less interested in speakers than in kinds of speakers, we abstract away from individual speaker choices to identify larger linguistic patterns: repeated uses of a marker or other linguistic resource that often perform shared social and grammatical functions. Of particular interest are patterns that repeat across generations, regions, and social situations. Their persistence reinforces their associations with socially defined communities and classes of grammar based on structural similarities. This, in turn, provides constructs such as African American English (AAE) with relatively stable identities useful in a wide range of analytical pursuits. African American use of the marker done in sentences like you done messed up plays a role in a number of such patterns. It has therefore figured prominently in characterizations of African American speech, with special attention often given to the marker’s use in expressing indignation and sass. Rather than locate such meanings in the semantics of the marker itself, the analysis of AAE done developed in this talk assigns the marker a relatively abstract semantics based on stativity. It leaves many, if not most, of the meanings commonly associated with done to be derived pragmatically by speakers. These include not only richer affective interpretations, such as indignation, but more grammatical interpretations, such as recency and completion. Because pragmatic interpretation depends on what speakers do with markers in context, the analysis brings speaker choice into clear view. In doing so, it may also help explain the persistence of done in part as a matter of conversational utility. By highlighting pragmatic choice in the use of this feature so strongly associated with African American language practices, the analysis aims to make visible the role of speaker agency in bringing social structure and grammatical organization together in actual language use.

events.title: GLNT: Arithmetic intersections on non-split Cartan modular curves
events.summary: Abstract: Take two CM elliptic curves over a number field, each equipped with a level structure preserved by all endomorphisms. At which primes $p$ does there exist an isomorphism between the elliptic curves mod $p$ that preserves the level structures? This question was answered for $\Gamma_0(N)$ level structure by Gross, Kohnen, and Zagier in 1987. A key step in their proof is showing that an isomorphism mod $p$ determines embeddings of the (quadratic) CM orders into a common (quaternion) Eichler order. In this talk, we will discuss what changes in the argument when we replace $\Gamma_0(N)$ with the normalizer of a non-split Cartan subgroup. This is joint work with Elie Studnia and Jan Vonk.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. Black Birth Joy Thursday, October 1, 2026 – Friday, January 15, 2027 Lane Hall Exhibit Space, 204 S State St., Ann Arbor, MI Open M–F, 9AM–5PM

events.title: MICDE State of AI: End-to-End Computational Scientific Discovery
events.summary: This special event will present a recent breakthrough by professors Kai Sun (Physics) and Venkat Viswanathan (Aerospace). Fractional Chern insulators are exotic topological states of matter that host anyons, a proposed foundation for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but their small energy gaps confine them to extremely low temperatures. The team asked frontier AI models to propose a new theoretical framework for topological flat bands, then set a swarm of agents to explore it, coordinating only through a shared message board, with every candidate checked by GPU-accelerated exact diagonalization. The swarm found a surprise: departing from the “ideal” quantum geometry long considered optimal raised the many-body gap more than tenfold over the starting bands, well past the previous benchmark and beyond what agents working alone reached. AI-assisted analysis then distilled this into a simple sheared Landau level model that explains the mechanism (reshaped electron orbitals stiffen the short-range repulsion protecting the state) and yields a design index computable without many-body simulation. Proposing the hypothesis, searching it, explaining what it found, and presenting a model offers an early look at end-to-end scientific discovery with AI.

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show
events.summary: Jack Tucker is hilariously awful, and that’s precisely the point. The Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show is the misguided brainchild of Zach Zucker, a performer who is celebrated for blending virtuosic clowning with razor-sharp satire. His character Jack Tucker is a well-respected journeyman and bonafide legend on the Upstate New York regional comedy scene, a catastrophically overconfident stand-up comedian whose hacky punchlines, misplaced swagger, and desperate need to be adored convince him that he’s going to make it big any day now. As his jokes collapse and his bravado frays, the show exposes the fragile ego beneath the spotlight and the quiet terror behind the mic. Equal parts parody, performance art, and masterclass in comedic tension, Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show walks a thrilling line, with Zach Zucker’s physical control and improvisational daring bringing both discipline and danger to the chaos. Zucker, whose clown lineage dates to the famous École Philippe Gaulier in France, the training ground for actors such as Sacha Baron Cohen, Helena Bonham Carter, Emma Thompson, and many others, is a cult favorite on the international comedy circuit, known for his always sold-out Stamptown Comedy and a forthcoming Netflix special. Recommended for mature audiences.

events.title: Missing Results of Discrimination: A Meta-Analysis of Racial, Gender, and Intersectional Discrimination Using Correspondence Audits
events.summary: CID Speaker Series Join the Stone Center for Inequality Dynamics as we host S. Michael Gaddis, clinical associate professor of management and policy in Georgia State University’s Andrew Young School of Policy Studies. Abstract: Intersectionality theory argues that race and gender cannot be fully understood in isolation or through an additive approach. This study introduces a systematically comparative framework for identifying missing results in correspondence audits and helping scholars conduct more holistic analyses. Drawing on 52 correspondence audits encompassing nearly 330,000 tests, it identifies patterns that can be missed when racial and gender discrimination are analyzed separately rather than through an intersectional framework, and offers best-practice recommendations for designing, analyzing, and citing correspondence audits. Gaddis is a methodologist with expertise in survey and experimental design whose research advances understanding of inequality and discrimination across multiple dimensions.

events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: Inverse problems over probability measure space
events.summary: Inverse problems are ubiquitous. Traditionally, the goal is to infer an unknown vector or function. But what if the unknown is a probability measure? Seeking a measure that generates data consistent with given observations leads to an optimization problem over probability space. However, the complex geometric nature of this space prevents the direct use of standard arguments and solvers. We unravel some of the surprises that emerge in this setting and discuss potential solutions.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*
