events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: Comics Beyond Sight
events.summary: This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening. View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

events.title: Ian Fink Trio
events.summary: Fri | Nov 13 Sets 7pm & 9pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE About the Artist Ian Finkelstein, who performs under the name Ian Fink, is a pianist, producer, composer and bandleader based in Detroit. Globally renowned for his lyricism, versatility, and musical fluency, Ian is a transcendent performer, sought after for his skills as a collaborator and session musician. Ian was taken under the wing of some of Detroit’s greatest educators and musicians, such as Marcus Belgrave and Rodney Whitaker, as a young teenager. He began to gig professionally at the age of 14, going on to study at the University of Michigan’s School of Music, Theater and Dance, where he was a student of the great Geri Allen. He received two BFAs in Jazz Piano Performance and Performing Arts Technology, graduating in 2013. With a firm foundation in the jazz piano tradition of Detroit, Ian was equally influenced by the city’s house and techno scene. He began to self-release music and press up vinyl in 2017, forming a record label entitled Freak Press, which contains a discography that is extensive and musically diverse, including but not limited to jazz, house, and ambient music. His recorded contributions can be heard on albums such as SICK! by Earl Sweatshirt (“Fire In The Hole”), ANIMALS by Kassa Overall (“Still Ain’t Find Me”) as well as on records by Black Milk, Shigeto, Robert Hurst, The Undisputed Truth, Scott Grooves, and more. He has performed with Marcus Belgrave, Benny Golson, Esperanza Spalding, Teri Lyne Carrington, Dee Dee Bridgewater, Common, Karriem Riggins, Savion Glover, Reggie Workman, Lenny White, Louis Hayes, Curtis Fuller and many others. He toured internationally with the Shigeto Live Ensemble in 2018 and 2019. Ian went on to become a member of Kassa Overall’s band from 2021 through 2024, including a February 2023 performance on NPR’s Tiny Desk Concerts. He is a regular member of Detroit bassist Robert Hurst’s band. In 2020, he was honored with a Gilda Award by Kresge Arts in Detroit, and in 2024 was awarded a Kresge Artist Fellowship. He was honored by the City of Detroit with a Spirit of Detroit Award and Testimonial Resolution in 2024. RESERVE TABLE

events.title: Algebraic Geometry Seminar: Stable map resolutions of Richardson varieties
events.summary: Given a circle action S on a projective variety X, we introduce the "stable map quotient" using Kontsevich's space of stable maps of curves. In the case that X is a Richardson variety (the intersection of a Schubert with an opposite Schubert variety), generally very singular, the quotient is nonetheless smooth! I'll use this to give a log resolution of Richardson varieties, and describe the dual simplicial complex to the anticanonical sncd boundary.

events.title: Notion in Ionia: An International Symposium at the University of Michigan
events.summary: The cultural history of Ionia in western Türkiye resonates with many of the major concerns of contemporary Mediterranean archaeology: the transition from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age; different modes of human mobility, including migration and colonization; interaction between the Greek world and the Near East, especially in the Persian era; the evolution of the city, in particular the Greek polis in the Hellenistic period; Roman imperialism and its effects on subject peoples; and religious and economic change in late antiquity. Recent research in the region of the Hales River valley, dominated by the inland city of Colophon, the port town of Notion, and the rural sanctuary of Apollo at Claros, has shed new light on all these subjects. This two-day symposium at the Kelsey Museum of Archaeology examines the results of ongoing survey and excavation at Notion in the context of its larger regional and supra-regional environments. Free and open to the public, the event will also focus on intellectual collaboration between Turkish and American students and scholars. +Learn+ more about the symposium at https://myumi.ch/Pb5PV. +View+ the full program at https://myumi.ch/G75bP. If you have any questions or concerns regarding accessing this event, please visit our accessibility page at https://myumi.ch/zwPkd or contact the education office by calling (734) 647-4167. We ask for advance notice as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: CSAS Lecture Series | What is the Private Life of Caste in India? The caste economies of India's success story
events.summary: Please note: This lecture will be held in person and virtually on Zoom. If you would like to attend via Zoom, registration is required. Once you've registered, joining information will be sent to your email. Register for the Zoom webinar at: https://myumi.ch/399y2 In this talk Thiranagama will draw from her book *The Monster in Your Path: The Private Life of Caste in India* on the situated histories of caste and enslavement in the South Indian state of Kerala, most often understood as India's success story. Thiranagama will discuss how new forms of caste disparities, as well as caste formations, have become sedimented not in the “public,” the center of most contemporary work, but rather in the new kinds of private spaces and private lives that arose after Kerala’s land reforms and communist transformation. Thiranagama suggests new ways to think about contemporary inequalities within historical economies of humiliation and subordination, as well discussing the dignity projects embarked upon by Kerala’s Dalit communities. Sharika Thiranagama is professor of anthropology at Stanford University. Her research explores violence, inequality, and intense political mobilization through a focus on intimacy, gender and generation. She has been the author of multiple works on Sri Lanka including *In My Mother’s House: Civil War in Sri Lanka* (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2011). Her most recent book *The Monster in Your Path* (University of California 2026) focuses on Dalit communities in Kerala, South India examining the gendered inheritance and life of enslavement, caste and work. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: AIM Seminar:  Quantum Gibbs Sampling: Mixing, Algorithm Design, and Measurement
events.summary: Abstract: Quantum Gibbs states describe the thermal equilibrium of quantum many-body systems and underlie many central questions in condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry. Preparing these states is a natural task for quantum computers, and a promising approach is quantum Gibbs sampling, which runs a quantum analogue of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) whose stationary state is the Gibbs state. In this talk, I will first introduce the basic ideas of quantum Gibbs sampling, drawing analogies with classical MCMC along the way, and then discuss three questions about these algorithms. First, how fast do they converge? For one-dimensional spin chains at any temperature, we show that a standard detailed-balanced quantum Gibbs sampler mixes in polylogarithmic time, using a spectral analysis that goes beyond the spectral gap. Second, can they be made simple? We construct samplers based on weakly coupling the system to a small bath, which avoids the heavy machinery of exact samplers. We show that a detailed-balance structure, together with randomized interaction times, removes the bias induced by the bath. Third, how do we read out the result? Instead of destroying the state at each measurement, we design non-destructive measurements that preserve, or nearly preserve, the Gibbs state, reducing the cost per sample from the full mixing time to the autocorrelation time. Contact: Zhiyan Ding

events.title: DAAS Faculty Forum with Justine Davis, Assistant Professor of Afroamerican and African Studies and Political Science
events.summary: Faculty members of the Department of Afroamerican and African Studies discuss their projects, research, and publications to share their work and interests. The DAAS Faculty Forum will be held monthly on Wednesdays at noon. October 21: Justine Davis, Assistant Professor of Afroamerican and African Studies; Assistant Professor of Political Science Dual Citizenship & Dueling Loyalties: Perceptions of Politicians from the Diaspora Abstract: How do citizens perceive and respond to dual citizenship and diaspora policies, particularly pertaining to politicians who have ties to multiple countries? This project entails a multi-country survey and experimental design in Côte d'Ivoire and Liberia on public opinion about dual citizenship. Given the growing political and economic influence of the African diaspora, the rights and roles of dual citizens have become increasingly contentious. Using a descriptive survey and a conjoint experiment, we explore when and why citizens support dual citizenship, how they respond to diaspora politicians, and how they view the role dual citizens and the broader diaspora play in the economic and democratic development of their countries. Bio: ​I am an assistant professor jointly appointed in the Department of Afroamerican and African Studies (DAAS) and the Political Science Department at the University of Michigan. Prior to this position, I was a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Michigan and a UC Presidential Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of California, San Diego. I received my Ph.D. in Political Science from the University of California, Berkeley. I study comparative politics and political behavior, focusing on sub-Saharan Africa. In particular, I am interested in the challenges of democratization efforts in post-conflict settings and weakly institutionalized democracies. My book, No Neutral Ground, forthcoming with Cambridge University Press, examines the role of non-governmental organizations in fostering democracy after civil war. My research has been supported by the Carnegie Corporation; the National Science Foundation; the West Africa Research Association; the Human Rights Center at UC Berkeley; and the Center for African Studies, the Peder Sather Center for Advanced Study, and the Institute for International Studies at UC Berkeley. My work has been featured on the Washington Post’s Monkey Cage and published or forthcoming in African Affairs, Comparative Political Studies, Journal of Conflict Resolution, Journal of Politics, Party Politics, Political Behavior, and PS: Political Science & Politics. At the University of Michigan, I am an associate at the African Studies Center and a faculty associate at the Center for Political Studies. I am a member of Evidence and Governance in Politics, a research associate at the Center on the Politics of Development, a co-coordinator of the Midwest Workshop in Empirical Political Science, a Ford Foundation Pre-Doctoral Fellow, and an APSA Diversity Fellow. I was also part of the 2023 Inaugural Class for The Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences (CASBS), Summer Institute on Diversity Science, at Stanford University. Prior to obtaining my Ph.D., I completed a Fulbright-Clinton Public Policy Fellowship in Côte d’Ivoire. I hold a dual-language Master's degree in International Affairs, Conflict Resolution and Civil Society Development from the American University of Paris and the Université de Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. Originally from North Carolina, I graduated from Elon University with a Bachelor's degree in International Studies, African concentration. Overall, I have experience living and working in France, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Senegal, and I have also conducted fieldwork in Zambia and Benin. Zoom link: https://umich.zoom.us/j/96271791304 November 18: Martin Murray, Adjunct Professor of Afroamerican and African Studies; Professor of Urban and Regional Planning, Alfred Taubman College of Architecture and Urban Planning

events.title: Biomedical Engineering (BME 500) Seminar Series
events.summary: At the Cell–Matrix Interface: Inflammatory Signaling and the Mechanobiology of Tendinopathy Abstract: Tendinopathy is a common and often persistent musculoskeletal disorder characterized by extracellular-matrix disorganization, altered tissue mechanics, and chronic inflammatory signaling. Yet the mechanisms linking changes in the extracellular matrix to sustained cellular dysfunction remain incompletely understood. This seminar will examine how nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling contributes to tendon degeneration and repair, with emphasis on the reciprocal relationship between tendon cells and their extracellular matrix. Using biomechanical, cellular, and preclinical models, our work shows that dysregulated NF-κB activity can drive chronic tendon pathology and impair healing, while targeted modulation of this pathway may improve tendon-to-bone repair. I will also discuss emerging evidence that matrix composition and mechanics shape fibroblast inflammatory responses, metabolism, and mechanosensing. Together, these studies position the cell–matrix interface as a critical regulator of tendinopathy and a promising target for therapeutic development.. Bio: Adam C. Abraham, PhD, is an Assistant Professor of Orthopaedic Surgery at the University of Michigan. Trained in mechanical engineering, biomedical engineering, musculoskeletal biology, and immunology, Dr. Abraham studies how mechanical loading, extracellular-matrix properties, and inflammatory signaling interact to regulate connective-tissue health and disease. His laboratory focuses on tendon mechanobiology and pathophysiology, particularly the role of cell–extracellular matrix interactions in controlling fibroblast behavior and chronic inflammation. Dr. Abraham’s research has helped establish NF-κB signaling as a mechanistic driver and potential therapeutic target in tendinopathy and tendon-to-bone healing. His current National Institutes of Health-funded work examines how the extracellular matrix regulates inflammatory signaling in tendon. By integrating multiscale biomechanics, engineered tissue models, and preclinical disease models, his research seeks to identify mechanisms that can be translated into improved treatments for tendon injury and degeneration.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Notion in Ionia: An International Symposium at the University of Michigan
events.summary: The cultural history of Ionia in western Türkiye resonates with many of the major concerns of contemporary Mediterranean archaeology: the transition from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age; different modes of human mobility, including migration and colonization; interaction between the Greek world and the Near East, especially in the Persian era; the evolution of the city, in particular the Greek polis in the Hellenistic period; Roman imperialism and its effects on subject peoples; and religious and economic change in late antiquity. Recent research in the region of the Hales River valley, dominated by the inland city of Colophon, the port town of Notion, and the rural sanctuary of Apollo at Claros, has shed new light on all these subjects. This two-day symposium at the Kelsey Museum of Archaeology examines the results of ongoing survey and excavation at Notion in the context of its larger regional and supra-regional environments. Free and open to the public, the event will also focus on intellectual collaboration between Turkish and American students and scholars. +Learn+ more about the symposium at https://myumi.ch/Pb5PV. +View+ the full program at https://myumi.ch/G75bP. If you have any questions or concerns regarding accessing this event, please visit our accessibility page at https://myumi.ch/zwPkd or contact the education office by calling (734) 647-4167. events.title: When AI Gets It Wrong: Learning Generative AI Through Its Mistakes
events.summary: Generative AI tools often make mistakes, especially with historical East Asian sources. This hands-on workshop, led by Kwok-leong Tang from Harvard University, uses those mistakes to explain how the technology works, so that participants can decide when to trust it and when to use it. No technical background is needed, and you can attend in person or register to join via Zoom (https://myumi.ch/zNnZM). A laptop is required for in-person participants — the Hatcher Gallery Lab is equipped with laptops, but please feel free to bring your own. When an AI tool gives a wrong answer, there are two possible reasons: the model itself cannot do the task, or we have not given it what it needs. The workshop teaches how to tell these apart. First, we will run a small AI model on our own laptops and look inside it: how it reads text, how it chooses each word, and why it can sound certain and still be wrong. Next, we will see how clearer instructions, more context, or a connected tool can fix some mistakes but not others. Finally, we will practice a simple way to test an AI answer: ask the same question several times and check the results against a reliable source. Kwok-leong Tang serves as the managing director of the Digital China Initiative and a lecturer for the Department of East Asian Languages and Civilizations at Harvard University. By training, he is a historian. He received his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in history from the Chinese University of Hong Kong and a Ph.D. in history and Asian Studies from Pennsylvania State University. In recent years, he has focused on exploring the potential of new technologies in humanities research. He has organized and instructed workshops on adopting GenAI in Chinese studies and humanities research at Harvard and other institutions. The Deep Dive into Digital and Data Methods for Chinese Studies series is sponsored by the U-M Library (Asia Library) and the Lieberthal-Rogel Center for Chinese Studies. For inquiries, please contact asialibrary@umich.edu.

ABOUT THE GUEST ARTIST Dr. Stowe has appeared in concert venues and music festivals in the Far East, Europe, South America, and throughout the United States and Canada, playing with some of the most prominent singers of his generation, including Randall Scarlata, Denyce Graves, Reginald Mobley, Susan Graham, Danielle DeNiese, Faith Esham, Vinson Cole, Sari Gruber, Jesse Blumberg, and Oral Moses. In addition, Stowe served as keynote speaker and artist-teacher at the first Chinese National Conference on Collaborative Piano. events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. Black Birth Joy Thursday, October 1, 2026 – Friday, January 15, 2027 Lane Hall Exhibit Space, 204 S State St., Ann Arbor, MI Open M–F, 9AM–5PM

events.title: IES Energy Seminar Series -  Hierarchy and Imperfect Competition in Power Markets afflicted by Uncertainty
events.summary: Abstract: Models for horizontal and hierarchical competition in power markets have been a source of significant interest over the last several decades. Yet less is known above computing equilibria in such settings particularly in the face of uncertainty. In this talk, we discuss flexible modeling paradigms for capturing Nash and Stackleberg equilibria in such settings. We briefly discuss computational methods for rigorous computation of equilibria in such settings. Time permitting, we pose some open questions in this setting. Biography: Uday V. Shanbhag is currently the Katta G. Murty Collegiate Professor and has been at the department of Industrial and Operations Engineering at the University of Michigan at Ann Arbor since Fall, 2024. From January 2017 to June 2024, he held the Gary and Sheila Chaired Professorsip in the department of Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering (IME) at the Pennsylvania State University, having been a tenured associate professor until 2016, since arriving in Fall 2012. Prior to being at Penn. State, from 2006–2012, he was first an assistant professor, and subsequently a tenured associate professor (for approx. 10 days), in the department of Industrial and Enterprise Systems engineering (ISE) at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC). He serves on the editorial boards of the SIAM Journal of Optimization, the Mathematics of Operations Research, Computational Optimization and its Applications, and the Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications. Uday V. Shanbhag has a Ph.D. from Stanford University's department of Management Science and Engineering (2006), with a concentration in operations research and was associated with the Systems Optimization Laboratory when at Stanford. He also holds masters (1998) and undergraduate (1993) degrees from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Cambridge (in Operations Research) and the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Bombay, respectively. events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Adam Lenhart, carillon
events.summary: Graduate student Adam Lenhart performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds. Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Comics Beyond Sight
events.summary: This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening. View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: CMENAS 2026 Fall Colloquium Series | ‘Vernacular Sovereignty’ Without a State: Kurdish Studies, Decolonial Thought, and the Making of Online Kurdistan
events.summary: What does it mean to imagine a nation without a state? This talk draws on my broader research in Kurdish studies to examine how Kurdish political life has repeatedly been organized around forms of authority and belonging that do not depend on, or wait for, a state. Taking my recent article "The Making of Online Kurdistan," co-authored with Barış Öktem, as its empirical center, the talk asks how Kurdish Generation Z constructs national belonging through digital platforms — building a transnational field of community through hashtags, online seminars, and digitally organized movements, even as this same infrastructure exposes Kurdish youth to surveillance and repression across borders. I situate this case within a longer arc of my work on Kurdish politics and within a decolonial reading of Kurdish studies more broadly. Rather than offering a general theory of sovereignty, the talk uses the Kurdish case to think through a live and unresolved question in the study of stateless nations: what forms can political authority, legitimacy, and collective imagination take when territorial statehood is foreclosed, and what is gained and lost when that struggle moves online. Mashuq Kurt is Associate Professor of Sociology in the Department of Law and Criminology at Royal Holloway, University of London. His work sits at the intersection of Middle Eastern studies and the sociology of migration and diaspora, examining how Kurds and other marginalised communities construct political authority and belonging outside the institutions of the nation-state. He is the author of *Kurdish Hizbullah in Turkey: Islamism, Violence and the State* (Pluto Press, 2017), co-editor of the *South Atlantic Quarterly Special Issue: Decolonizing Kurdish Studies *(2024) and the *Contemporary Islam Special Issue: Islam, Critique and the Canon* (2024), and has published in journals including *Current Anthropology*, *Journal of Middle East Women's Studies*, and *Social Research: An International Quarterly*. His recent article "The Making of Online Kurdistan" (*Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies*, 2026), co-authored with Barış Öktem, examines how Kurdish Generation Z constructs national belonging through digital platforms. He was a Marie Curie Global Fellow at the London School of Economics and Yale University, has held visiting positions at Stanford and Sciences Po CERI. A regular contributor to public and policy debates, he has organised panels and given talks at the UK Parliament, Chatham House, and RUSI, and his commentary has appeared in Foreign Policy, Le Monde, and The New Arab, among others. He is also an award-winning filmmaker: his documentary *The Seven Doors *received the Jean Rouch Award from the American Anthropological Association's Society for Visual Anthropology in 2020. Join on Zoom: https://myumi.ch/pgV2y If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange. Contact: warsansa@umich.edu *Part of the International Institute Theme Year: Sovereignty* https://myumi.ch/ii-theme

events.title: Ian Fink Trio
events.summary: Fri | Nov 13 Sets 7pm & 9pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE About the Artist Ian Finkelstein, who performs under the name Ian Fink, is a pianist, producer, composer and bandleader based in Detroit. Globally renowned for his lyricism, versatility, and musical fluency, Ian is a transcendent performer, sought after for his skills as a collaborator and session musician. Ian was taken under the wing of some of Detroit’s greatest educators and musicians, such as Marcus Belgrave and Rodney Whitaker, as a young teenager. He began to gig professionally at the age of 14, going on to study at the University of Michigan’s School of Music, Theater and Dance, where he was a student of the great Geri Allen. He received two BFAs in Jazz Piano Performance and Performing Arts Technology, graduating in 2013. With a firm foundation in the jazz piano tradition of Detroit, Ian was equally influenced by the city’s house and techno scene. He began to self-release music and press up vinyl in 2017, forming a record label entitled Freak Press, which contains a discography that is extensive and musically diverse, including but not limited to jazz, house, and ambient music. His recorded contributions can be heard on albums such as SICK! by Earl Sweatshirt (“Fire In The Hole”), ANIMALS by Kassa Overall (“Still Ain’t Find Me”) as well as on records by Black Milk, Shigeto, Robert Hurst, The Undisputed Truth, Scott Grooves, and more. He has performed with Marcus Belgrave, Benny Golson, Esperanza Spalding, Teri Lyne Carrington, Dee Dee Bridgewater, Common, Karriem Riggins, Savion Glover, Reggie Workman, Lenny White, Louis Hayes, Curtis Fuller and many others. He toured internationally with the Shigeto Live Ensemble in 2018 and 2019. Ian went on to become a member of Kassa Overall’s band from 2021 through 2024, including a February 2023 performance on NPR’s Tiny Desk Concerts. He is a regular member of Detroit bassist Robert Hurst’s band. In 2020, he was honored with a Gilda Award by Kresge Arts in Detroit, and in 2024 was awarded a Kresge Artist Fellowship. He was honored by the City of Detroit with a Spirit of Detroit Award and Testimonial Resolution in 2024. RESERVE TABLE

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
events.summary: Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering. As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting? On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

William Hill III is a pianist, composer, arranger, and bandleader based in New York City hailing from Detroit, Michigan. Hill is a graduate of the Detroit School of Arts (Class of 2022) and a recent graduate of Manhattan School of Music with a bachelor of music degree (Class of 2026). He will continue his education in the fall as a graduate student at The Juilliard School (Class of 2028). Hill has had the opportunity to participate in many summer extensive jazz camps such as Jazz House Kids, Jr. Jazz Academy at Lincoln Center, Berklee Summer Programs, Interlochen Center for the Arts, Motown Lyric Project, Keeping an Eye Summer Jazz Workshop located at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam, Betty Carter’s Jazz Ahead, and many others. Hill is honored to receive awards from programs such as the National YoungArts Foundation, a multi-year winner in the instrumental contemporary category for the NAACP ACT-SO National Competition, and the West Virginia Univeristy International Jazz Piano Competition. Musicians that Hill has worked alongside and have been mentored by include Marc Cary, Aaron Parks, Buster Williams, Christian McBride, Jaleel Shaw, Jazzmeia Horn, Joe Farnsworth, Ari Hoenig, Jason Moran, Rodney Whitaker, Wynton Marsalis, and many more. Hill has had the opportunity to perform at the 46th Annual Detroit Jazz Festival, 2026 Jazz Congress, Unity Jazz Festival, Winter Jazz Festival, Dizzy’s Club, Smalls Jazz Club, Mezzrow Jazz Club,Minton’s Playhouse, The Kennedy Center, Esplanade-Theaters on the B ay (Singapore), Blue Note Tokyo, and many others to name a few. Hill has recently released his sophomore album, “Keep it Movin’” summer of 2025. Hill’s passion in life as a musician is to spread joy to everyone around the world with the music that he produces.

events.title: Jia Yi Gu & Kate Yeh Chiu
events.summary: Material Feast Material Feast is an interdisciplinary dialogue featuring designers and practitioners interrogating the contemporary role of materials in design. Framed as a “feast,” a term that gestures toward sensory abundance, the event invites us to consider materials as processes rather than products. Designers Brittanie Dabney, Catie Newell, Meredith Miller, Melanie McClintock, and Ana Morcillo Pallarés will each give a brief presentation of their practice, using provisional objects and material samples to probe the boundaries between art, science, design, and craft. Alongside the presentations, a material library will bring together samples drawn from automotive plastic waste streams, quagga mussels from lake systems, and waste glass, as well as perforated textiles, hydrogels, and brittle sponges made from foraged “kin” species. Organized by Material Acts Material Feast is organized by Material Acts (Kate Yeh Chiu, Jia Yi Gu and Hilary Huckins-Weidner), a research platform exploring materials as cultural technique through public events centering an experimental library. The project attends to the logistical, economic, and technological actions that transform matter into the material substrate for our lives. Initiated in 2021 as part of Getty PST ART, the project has taken the form of a major exhibition at Craft Contemporary, an editorial project with e-flux Architecture, and a publication of ideas, conversations, and material inquiries. Working through exhibitions, programming, and editorial projects, Material Acts brings together theoretical and practical engagements with materials, addressing how design and architecture are entangled with social and ecological concerns. www.materialacts.org Contributors Brittanie Dabney Brittanie Dabney is the founder and CEO of Ecosphere Organics, a Detroit-based company that converts food waste from local restaurants and suppliers into reusable materials. An environmental scientist trained at Wayne State University, she studied microplastic pollution, and her company now develops compostable packaging and plant-based leather alternatives at Newlab. She is adjunct faculty at the College for Creative Studies and served on the 2025 Detroit Month of Design curatorial committee. Catie Newell Catie Newell is Professor of Architecture at the University of Michigan's Taubman College, which she joined in 2009 as the Oberdick Fellow. She is the founding principal of Alibi Studio, established in Detroit in 2010, and her work explores materiality in relation to place through material systems, light, and darkness. She is a Lucas Fellow, a Kresge Artist Fellow, and a Fellow of the American Academy in Rome. Meredith Miller Meredith Miller is Associate Professor of Architecture and Director of the Master of Architecture program at Taubman College. She holds a BS from the University of Virginia and a Master of Architecture from Princeton. With Thom Moran, she leads Post Rock, a research initiative developing a composite building product from waste plastics, and she is a founding member of the practice T+E+A+M. Melanie McClintock Melanie McClintock is Chair of Color & Materials Design at the College for Creative Studies, with an MFA from CCS and a BFA in Fashion Design from Virginia Commonwealth University. A CMF designer, multi-media artist, curator, and educator, she explores material-driven concepts of time, worthiness, and a sense of place. She worked in the fashion industry for over two decades in the United States, Qatar, and Indonesia. Ana Morcillo Pallarés Ana Morcillo Pallarés is an architect, designer, and researcher and Associate Professor of Architecture at Taubman College, teaching architectural design, design research, and spatial politics. She holds a PhD in architecture from Taubman and is developing research on the natural thermal properties of the biomatter of the quagga mussel as an opportunity for the fabrication of alternative by-products for the architectural residential industry. She is principal of Rumor Studio, formerly Morcillo Pallarés + Rule Arquitectos.

events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. Black Birth Joy Thursday, October 1, 2026 – Friday, January 15, 2027 Lane Hall Exhibit Space, 204 S State St., Ann Arbor, MI Open M–F, 9AM–5PM

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.title: Jessi Grieser, carillon
events.summary: LSA faculty member Jessi Grieser performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

events.title: Citations Beyond “Playing the Game:” Building a Robust Citation Policy
events.summary: In this workshop, participants will bring a personal research project to assess or map out a citation policy that reflects their commitments and values. Sara Ahmed tells us that “citations can be feminist bricks: they are the materials through which, from which, we create our dwellings.” Our citation policies “affec[t] the kind of house” in which we spend our intellectual lives (Living a Feminist Life 15). In this workshop, participants begin by reflecting on their various commitments and values before engaging in a discussion of the shared reading. The session concludes with individual and collaborative workshop time targeting feasibility in their designs. Participants assess citations in a recent project to determine the extent to which they have used citations to build the kind of “dwelling” they want to occupy and explore options for further renovating. Qualifiers: This is a workshop especially designed for those in the humanities, social and applied sciences. events.title: The Limits of Targeted Hiring Subsidies: Evidence from the Work Opportunity Tax Credit (joint with Manisha Jain and Jeffrey Weaver)
events.summary: Employer-side wage subsidies are widely used to promote employment among disadvantaged workers. We study how such subsidies translate into firm hiring behavior using the federal Work Opportunity Tax Credit, which subsidizes up to 40% of first-year wages and covers over two million hires annually. Using linked administrative data from Wisconsin and multiple quasi- experimental designs, we find consistent and precise null effects on hiring, earnings, retention, and related outcomes across designs and firm types. Original data on firm hiring practices suggest two mechanisms that can limit employer-side subsidy efficacy: perceived legal risks discourage eligibility screening and organizational frictions attenuate decision-makers’ responsiveness.

Though his engagements may include jazz clubs to music halls and jazz festivals, he takes the time to contribute to his home music scene through mentorship and appearances with up-and-coming talents. He has appeared on stage alongside Donald Byrd, Joe Lovano, Robert Hurst, JD Allen, Carla Cook, Bobby Lavell, Bob Moses, and Allen Vizzutti; toured with Stacy Dillard, Duane Eubanks and Noah Preminger; has performed with the Springfield Symphony Orchestra; and his latest album features the jazz bass legend Robert Hurst. He was the acting director of the Cornell University Jazz Ensembles in 2000-2001, during which time he welcomed Donald Byrd, Jimmy Heath, Wycliffe Gordon, Terell Stafford, Vincent Herring, and Joe Chambers onto the stage as guest soloists. events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Biomedical Engineering (BME 500) Seminar Series
events.summary: Making Learning Visible: Reflection, GenAI, and Measurement in Authentic Learning Environments Abstract: Authentic learning environments, such as capstone design or undergraduate research experiences, give engineering students opportunities to practice being an engineer. These learning environments are often characterized by students needing to navigate uncertainty, exercise judgment, and learn through collaboration. Yet measuring this learning is challenging, particularly across engineering’s diverse educational contexts. Students’ written reflections offer both a way to support learning and a window into how they make sense of their experiences. How can we use these rich, traditionally qualitative accounts to investigate patterns in learning across students and settings? Our research addresses four connected challenges: eliciting substantive reflection, establishing what students’ accounts can tell us about the learning we value, interpreting those accounts reliably, and producing findings that can inform educational practice. This seminar focuses on developing methods and tools that elicit deeper student reflection and support reliable analysis, drawing on both pedagogical design and new capabilities of generative AI. I will share work exploring AI-personalized short-form reflections and longer reflective memos, alongside human and AI-assisted approaches to analyzing students’ writing. These examples bring questions of validation, interrater reliability, and the role of course context into focus. Together, they contribute to a broader effort to develop measurement approaches that preserve the richness of students’ experiences while supporting research across learning environments and helping instructors improve their own courses. Bio: Alexandra Werth is an assistant professor in Cornell University’s Meinig School of Biomedical Engineering and a core faculty member of the Duffield Engineering Education Research Institute. She directs the Biomedical Engineering Education, Assessment, and Research (BEEAR) Lab, where her group studies how students learn and develop as engineers through research, design, and other authentic learning experiences. Her work examines reflection, feedback, and teamwork while developing human and generative AI-assisted methods for studying learning across educational contexts. She leads NSF-funded projects on AI-augmented reflection and pedagogical practices for engineering teamwork and received Cornell Engineering’s 2025 EPICC Award for Innovation. Werth holds bachelor’s degrees in engineering and physics from Swarthmore College and a Ph.D. in Electrical and Computer Engineering from Princeton University, where her research focused on noninvasive glucose sensing using quantum cascade laser spectroscopy. She subsequently conducted postdoctoral research in physics education at the University of Colorado Boulder, studying undergraduate laboratory learning and helping developed the first large-enrollment introductory physics course-based undergraduate research experience.

events.title: AI Futures Keynote: Isabelle Hau
events.summary: The Industrial Revolution elevated IQ, the cognitive abilities needed for an economy built around knowledge and analytical skill. The late 20th century expanded our understanding through EQ, recognizing the importance of understanding ourselves and others. Now, the AI revolution calls for another evolution in human intelligence: Relational Intelligence (RQ), our capacity to build trust, make meaning together, connect across differences, collaborate, navigate conflict, and repair. Universities have a critical role in this transition. As they prepare students for an AI-shaped future, they must revisit not only what we teach and how we learn, but how we relate, developing AI fluency alongside the deeply human capacities that will matter even more in an age of intelligent machines. This session asks a defining question: If AI changes what it means to be intelligent, how should education evolve what we teach, what we measure, and what we value? *About AI Futures Keynote Speaker Series* The Center for Academic Innovation is convening leading voices in academia to examine emerging applications of artificial intelligence in higher education. The AI Futures keynote speaker series is a critical examination of how artificial intelligence is reshaping teaching and learning as we consider the future of life changing education at Michigan

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.summary: Join us for a screening of “Hard to Swallow,” an award-winning docuseries chronicling the work and perspective of Nigerian chef and food writer Tunde Wey in collaboration with filmmaker Theo Schear. Essayistic and reflexive, “Hard to Swallow” recounts Wey’s explosive career while building a critique of the social structures that disenfranchise Black peoples globally. Through episodes that follow Wey from New Orleans’ food scene to Detroit’s mayor’s office to the show’s contentious debut in Cannes, “Hard to Swallow” is unlike any food show on air right now. Following the screening, prominent Detroit-based chef Ederique “Chef E” Goudia will moderate a discussion with show creators Wey and Schear.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.
events.imageAlt: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.
